title: Getting Started With Quarto
text:
About this resource
This is a Quarto book is for academic staff who want to get started using Quarto. We cover:

basic installation and building your first Quarto project
tips for migrating from a LaTeX source
using Quarto with a focus on lecture note things like: maths, figures, referencing and much more!







Tip



If you prefer, the Quarto website has a more complete set of information and examples: the purpose of this guide is to provide a more focused and practical introduction to Quarto for academic staff.








Note



This guide introduces the fundamentals of Quarto using a Visual Studio Code (VS Code) workflow.
Alternatively you can also use Quarto through RStudio (e.g. see Quarto for Scientists - an R Studio Workflow), the command line and other routes too!








NoteFeedback?



If you have any feedback or suggestion on how to make this book more useful then please get in touch with Josh Lim - University of Bath.
In particular I’d welcome:

Errors or corrections
Calls for clarification
Missing info
Suggestions for improvements/new topics

title: 1  What is Quarto?
text:
1.1 Why Use Quarto?
Quarto is a modern publishing system that allows you to create teaching materials from simple plain-text source files and publish them to a range of formats including:

title: 1  What is Quarto?
text:
1.1.1 Write Once, Publish Anywhere
A single source document can be rendered as:

A website for online reading
A printable PDF
A Word document
Presentation slides



1.1.2 Accessible formats
HTML output can provide:

Responsive design
Screen reader support
Improved navigation
Adjustable text size
Better support for mobile devices (compared to PDFs)



1.1.3 Plain Text Source Files
Quarto files are plain text, making them:

Easy to edit
Easy to archive
Suitable for version control systems such as Git
Portable across operating systems







Note



If you’re from a LaTeX background or bookdown then you’ll find the equation syntax and referencing familiar (citations can be managed with a .bib file).
However, given how extensible LaTeX is, you won’t have access to all the packages you may be familiar with.




1.1.4 Rich content
You can:

embed content (e.g. video, interactive widgets)
execute code and render outputs (e.g. Python, R)

title: 1  What is Quarto?
section: 1.2 The anatomy of a Quarto project
text:
1.2 The anatomy of a Quarto project
A typical Quarto project consists of:

A project folder
A _quarto.yml configuration file that sets project-level settings (e.g. formatting options, output formats). Similar to a LaTeX preamble, it’s useful to have this separately from the source files so you can easily re-use it.
One or more Quarto source files (with the extension .qmd). This is written in markdown and is the main bulk of your document.
a folder for images and other resources

Optionally, you may also include: - a bibliography file (with the extension .bib) for citations - a folder for custom scripts (e.g. Python, R) that can be executed during the rendering process - a folder for custom extensions (e.g. for new output formats or features - see Quarto extensions)

title: 1  What is Quarto?
text:
1.3 The Quarto stack
Quarto helps automate the process of converting your source content and configuration into a range of publication formats. You write your content in a .qmd file and control how it is rendered using YAML settings (either within the document or in project-level .yml files). Quarto then takes care of the remaining steps, so you can focus on writing content rather than managing complex publishing workflows.
Rendering workflow

You write content in a .qmd file using Markdown, equations, images, and optional code (e.g. additional .py, .R, .ipynb files).
You define settings using YAML metadata (your _quarto.yml file or a YAML block within the document).
Quarto executes code (if present) using Knitr, Jupyter, or another supported engine.
Quarto converts content using Pandoc.
Quarto generates final output in one or more formats. This includes HTML books (like this one), PDF documents (via LaTeX) and other formats (e.g. Word, Reveal.js, EPUB)

In practice, most authors only need to maintain their .qmd files and YAML settings (steps 1 and 2 above). Quarto automates the execution, conversion, and creation steps, allowing you to create professional outputs from a single source document.

You can render your project by:

You can either use the Terminal in VSCode (or just have a terminal open) and render the document from a terminal using:
quarto render






Tip



Alternatively, you can launch a live preview which automatically updates as you edit your content.

3.2.3 Quick preview
For a quick preview of simple markdown code, the Markdown All in One VSCode extension, will show an instant preview of any single markdown document. You can run this Preview from the VSCode command palette of Ctrl-Shift-V






Warning



Please note the quick preview is just a simple markdown display preview (it won’t know about references, figures, code) and doesn’t rebuild your whole project, but can be useful for quick previews to check things look roughly right.








Note

title: 5  Converting existing LaTeX Notes
text:
5.2 Automatically converting LaTeX
Pandoc can convert between lots of different formats including LaTeX (.tex) and Quarto (.qmd). It won’t do a perfect job and which is why it’s recommended to carefully go through your TeX source. However if your TeX is relatively clean (few macros, extra packages, complex float layouts), then Pandoc can get you going quite quickly.
From the command line you can run
pandoc -f latex -t markdown input-tex.tex -o output-md.qmd






Important



You will need to review the output .qmd to make sure you have output that is compatible.








Caution



Pandoc is not aware of your whole TeX project: you need to convert each .TeX separarely.

title: 5  Converting existing LaTeX Notes
text:
5.3 Tidying up the .qmd file
Here are some things Pandoc does not readily convert into markdown:

Section etc labels - if you used underscores in any of your latex labels you should change these to ‘-’ in the markdown file. The underscores confuse markdown. Chapter 9 discusses sections, chapters, etc.
Figures - the default pandoc conversion is quite limited, so here we’ll use a more adaptable figure environment. In practice its easiest to just copy-paste the example code in Chapter 6.
Equations - most equations convert fine but if you want to have equation numbers and labels you’ll need to do some tidying. See Chapter 7 for the syntax.
Tables - tables have a different format but it’s pretty easy to convert a latex table using find/replace or online table editors/converters (e.g. Table Convert) References - generally easy to fix - see Chapter 10

This list is based on the Making Lecture Notes with Bookdown guide by Vicky Scowcroft






Tip



If you’re from a LaTeX background and are editing/writing a Quarto document, you may sometimes forget to add blank lines between markdown commands (as with LaTeX you could just close brackets and define the next command). Some typical mistakes a LaTeX user makes in markdown:

you have a figure and then a paragraph of text, you must add a blank line between the figure and the paragraph. Otherwise the paragraph will be treated as part of the figure caption.
you start a list without a blank line, the list will be treated as part of the previous paragraph (and not start the list environment).

Simple tip Always add a blank line between different elements in your Quarto document. This will help avoid formatting issues!

title: 8  Code
text:
8.1 Including inline code snippets
Quarto supports executable code, code examples, and syntax-highlighted snippets for a wide range of programming languages. This makes it ideal for creating teaching materials, laboratory manuals, lecture notes, and technical documentation.
You can include inline code snippets in between single backticks, e.g. `print("Hello, world!")` (this renders as print("Hello, world!")).

title: 8  Code
text:
8.2 Including code blocks
You can include code blocks in triple backticks, followed by the language name (for syntax highlighting). For example:
```python
print("Hello, world!")
```
This results in the following rendered code output with syntax highlighting:
print("Hello, world!")






Tip



Supported languages for syntax highlighting include: Python, R, Bash, C, C++, Java, JavaScript, MATLAB, markdown and many more. See the Quarto documentation for a full list of supported languages.
For completely unformatted text use the ```text option.

title: 8  Code
text:
8.3 Running Code
Executable code is placed inside a code chunk (notice the curly braces after the opening triple backticks). You can specify the programming language for the code chunk (e.g. python, r, julia, bash, etc.) and Quarto will automatically highlight the syntax.
```{python}
print("Hello, world!")
```
This results in the following rendered output (shows code and output):

print("Hello, world!")

Hello, world!

title: 8  Code
text:
8.4 Options for running code
You can control how code is executed and displayed using chunk options. For example, you can hide the code but show the output, or hide both the code and the output. You can also control whether warnings and messages are displayed.
You can set chunk options for individual code chunks using the #| syntax directly after the opening triple backticks.

8.4.1 Showing output but hiding code
You can run the code and display the output, but hide the code source from viewers with #| echo: false
```{python}
#| echo: false
print("Only the output will appear.")
```
This results in the following rendered output:


Only the output will appear.




8.4.2 Folding Long Code Blocks
Long code examples can be collapsed to avoid cluttering the document with #| code-fold: true. You can also add a summary to the code block with #| code-summary: "Show Python code".
```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Python code"
print("This code is initially hidden.")
```
This results in the following rendered output:


Show Python code
print("This code is initially hidden.")


This code is initially hidden.








Note



The folding code blocks are expanded in the static PDF output.








Tip



It’s a good idea to keep code lines short (e.g. < 80 characters) as the LaTeX output does not wrap long lines of code.

title: 8  Code
text:
8.5 Figures from code
Figures generated from Python, R, or Julia code are automatically treated as figures. To make these accessible, you should include:

#| label: fig-line-plot - this gives a reference label to the figure
#| fig-cap: "A simple line plot" - this gives a figure caption
#| fig-alt: "Descriptive alt text" - this gives alternative text for accessibility (e.g. screen readers)

For example, the following code chunk generates a simple line plot:
```{python}
#| label: fig-line-plot
#| fig-cap: "A simple line plot"
#| fig-alt: "Line graph showing values increasing and decreasing across four observations."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.plot([1, 23, 2, 4])
plt.show()
```
This results in the following rendered output:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.plot([1, 23, 2, 4])
plt.show()







Figure 8.1: A simple line plot











Tip



Often it’s useful to add #| echo: false (see Section 8.4.1) at the start of the figure. This makes sure to not echo the code and only display the figure:
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-line-plot-noecho
#| fig-cap: "A simple line plot"
#| fig-alt: "A simplified plot with the#| echo: falseto not show the code"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.plot([1, 23, 2, 4])
plt.show()
```








Figure 8.2: A simple line plot

title: 8  Code
text:
8.6 Global Code Options
Chunk options can be applied to every code block using the document YAML.
---
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
---

title: 9  Working with sections
text:
9.1 How sections are displayed
Section headings create document structure automatically.
Quarto can automatically number sections using:
Each separate .qmd file will appear in the left hand navigation menu as a (numbered) chapter.
Within each .qmd, each heading level will appear in the table of contents (right hand side)

title: 9  Working with sections
text:
Heading level 1 # will increment the number (e.g. 1,2,3 etc)
Heading level 2 ## will increment the subpoints (e.g. 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 etc)
Heading level 3 ### will increment the sub-subpoint (e.g. 1.1.1, 1.1.2, 1.1.3 etc)

title: 9  Working with sections
text:
9.2 Numbering sections
Sections are numbered by default (# Section heading). You can create a unnumbered heading with {.unnumbered} (e.g. )# Unnumbered section heading {.unnumbered})

title: 9  Working with sections
text:
9.3 Global defaults
Numbered sections are the default and can be controlled in the yaml
format:
  html:
    number-sections: true
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
    toc-location: right
  pdf:
    number-sections: true

Sections can be assigned identifiers.

title: 10  References and citations
text:
10.1 Connecting the bibliography
Quarto supports citation management through BibTeX and a .bib file in the normal way.
Add the bibliography file to your YAML:

text:

csl: harvard-university-of-bath.csl
---






Note



A copy of the Harvard Bath style file is included in these notes.

title: 10  References and citations
text:
10.2 Citing Sources
Citations can be added using citation keys.
A single citation for literate programming @knuth84.
A single citation for literate programming Knuth (1984).
Multiple citations:
Multiple citations can be cited like this [@knuth84; @le2026quarto]. 
Multiple citations can be cited like this (Knuth 1984; Le Foll 2026).

text:
10.3 Reference list
A reference list is generated automatically at the end of each chapter page in the HTML output. However, in the PDF/docx output, the reference list is generated at the end of the document.

11.6 Quarto extensions
Quarto extensions are a way to add new features to Quarto. They can be used to create new output formats, add new functionality, or customize the behavior of Quarto.
See the Quarto extensions guidance for a list of extensions and how to create your own.

title: 12  Tweaking the YAML header
text:
12.1 Table of Contents
The YAML block appears at the top of every Quarto document.
A simple example:
Enable a table of contents:

    toc: true

title: 12  Tweaking the YAML header
text:
12.3 Themes
Quarto provides several built-in themes.
format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
Other popular themes include:

flatly
litera
united
lumen
sandstone

If you specify a light and dark theme, then Quarto will add in a toggle button to allow users to switch.
format:
  html:
    theme:
      light: cosmo
      dark: darkly






Caution



If you use dark mode, please if you images have transparency (if you have black text on a transparent background this can be illegible).

title: 12  Tweaking the YAML header
text:
12.4 Multiple Output Formats
Quarto can render several formats from the same source.
format:
  html:
    toc: true
  pdf:
    toc: true
  docx: default
Rendering the document then produces HTML, PDF, Word simultaneously.






Caution



Always check each output. Sometimes things may note always compile as you wish!

title: 12  Tweaking the YAML header
text:
12.5 Creating Books and Lecture Notes
A common approach is to keep all chapter files in a dedicated chapters folder and store chapter-specific images in an images directory within that folder.
project:
  type: book
Example structure:
course-notes/
│
├── _quarto.yml
├── index.qmd
├── references.bib
│
└── chapters/
    ├── week1.qmd
    ├── week2.qmd
    ├── week3.qmd
    │
    └── images/
        ├── lecture-diagram.png
        ├── experiment-setup.jpg
        └── results-plot.svg
Example _quarto.yml:
project:
  type: book
 
book:
  title: "Physics 1A Lecture Notes"
 
chapters:
- index.qmd
- chapters/week1.qmd
- chapters/week2.qmd
- chapters/week3.qmd

title: 13  Publishing a Quarto project
text:
13.1 Publish to Moodle
Once you have created your Quarto project, you will need to publish the rendered output so that others can access it. Quarto supports several publishing options, but for most teaching-related content at the University of Bath, publishing to Moodle is the recommended approach.
For teaching materials intended for University of Bath students, we recommend publishing your Quarto website or mini-site through Moodle.
Benefits include:
Quarto websites generate a collection of HTML, CSS, JavaScript, image, and supporting files. These can be hosted within Moodle as a self-contained mini-site.

title: 13  Publishing a Quarto project
text:
Available directly to students through Moodle.
Included within the University’s Moodle archive processes.
Covered by established institutional retention arrangements.
Access controlled through Moodle course permissions.
No requirement for students to visit external websites.



13.1.1 Moodle publishing workflow

Render your Quarto project.
Locate the generated _site or output folder.
Create a ZIP archive containing the entire published site and all supporting files.
In Moodle, create a File activity (not a Folder activity).
Upload the ZIP file and use Moodle’s Unzip option.
Set the site’s index.html file as the Main File.
Save the activity and test that the site launches correctly.

The University of Bath Moodle currently has a 50 MB upload limit for file activities. If your published site exceeds this size please contact tel@bath.ac.uk






Important



Detailed step-by-step guidance is available at Publishing an HTML mini-site to Moodle




13.1.2 Updating a Moodle-hosted site
When you make changes to your Quarto project:

Re-render the site locally.
Create a new ZIP archive of the updated output.
Replace the all existing files in Moodle.
Ensure the correct index.html file remains set as the Main File.

title: 13  Publishing a Quarto project
text:
13.2 Public Resources: GitHub Pages
If your Quarto content is intended for public access, GitHub Pages is an excellent option (no Moodle authentication required).
Advantages include:

Free hosting.
Integrated version control through Git.
Collaborative authoring workflows.
Automatic publishing when content is updated.
Suitable for open educational resources, documentation, and public-facing guides.







Tip



Github pages looks for html either in a docs folder or the root of the repo. It’s a good idea to update your yaml accordingly:
project:
  type: book
  output-dir: docs

title: Appendix A — Adding Jupyter Notebooks Chapters
text:
A.1 Adding a Notebook to the Quarto Book
Quarto can include Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) directly as book chapters. This is particularly useful when teaching materials combine narrative text, executable code, and visualisations created in Jupyter Notebook and you want to share it with students.
List the notebook in the chapters section of _quarto.yml just as you would a .qmd file (see Section 12.5).
Quarto will automatically render the notebook as a chapter in the book and include it in the table of contents and navigation.

title: Appendix A — Adding Jupyter Notebooks Chapters
text:
A.2 Controlling Code Display
Notebook cells can be shown, hidden, or folded using cell metadata.
For example, to hide a code cell while displaying its output:
{
  "tags": ["hide-input"]
}
Common tags include:

hide-input – hide code, show output
hide-output – show code, hide output
hide-cell – hide both code and output

text:
A.3 Using Notebooks with Quarto Features
Jupyter notebooks support many Quarto features, including:

Citations
Equations
Figure captions
Callouts
Cross-references
